metadata.title: Understanding deep learning requires rethinking generalization
metadata.authors: Chiyuan Zhang, Samy Bengio, Moritz Hardt, Benjamin Recht, Oriol Vinyals

nodes.name: Generalization error
nodes.statement: The generalization error of a model is the difference between its training error and its test error.
nodes.statement_clean: Difference between training and test error.

nodes.name: Effective capacity
nodes.statement: The effective model capacity is operationally measured by the model's ability to fit arbitrary (random) labelings of a finite training sample under the standard training procedure.
nodes.statement_clean: Operational notion of capacity: ability to fit random labelings via SGD.

nodes.name: Empirical Rademacher complexity
nodes.statement: For a hypothesis class $H$ on a dataset $\{x_1,\dots,x_n\}$, $\hat{R}_n(H) = \mathbb{E}_\sigma\left[\sup_{h\in H} \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \sigma_i h(x_i)\right]$ where $\sigma_i \in \{\pm 1\}$ are i.i.d. uniform.
nodes.statement_clean: Expected supremum of correlation between class members and random sign labels.

nodes.name: Uniform stability
nodes.statement: Uniform stability of an algorithm $A$ measures how sensitive $A$ is to the replacement of a single training example, and is solely a property of the algorithm independent of data distribution and labels.
nodes.statement_clean: Algorithm-only sensitivity to single-sample replacement.

nodes.name: Finite-sample expressivity
nodes.statement: A network $C$ can represent any function on a sample of size $n$ in $d$ dimensions if for every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ with $|S|=n$ and every $f: S \to \mathbb{R}$, there exist weights making $C(x)=f(x)$ for all $x \in S$.
nodes.statement_clean: Network can match any target on every n-point sample in $\mathbb{R}^d$.

nodes.name: Randomization test
nodes.statement: Variant of the non-parametric randomization test: train a fixed architecture on the original data and on a copy where labels (or pixels) are replaced by random ones, then compare training/test behavior.
nodes.statement_clean: Train on real vs randomized labels/pixels and compare.

nodes.name: ERM problem for linear models
nodes.section: 5 Implicit Regularization: An Appeal to Linear Models
nodes.statement: $\min_{w \in \mathbb{R}^d} \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathrm{loss}(w^T x_i, y_i)$
nodes.statement_clean: Empirical risk minimization for linear predictors.

nodes.name: Kernel system $XX^T \alpha = y$
nodes.section: 5 Implicit Regularization: An Appeal to Linear Models
nodes.statement: $XX^T \alpha = y$, the unique linear system characterizing the SGD-from-zero solution that interpolates the labels and lies in the span of the data.
nodes.statement_clean: Kernel-trick equation for SGD's interpolating linear solution.

nodes.name: Hessian of linear ERM
nodes.section: 5 Implicit Regularization: An Appeal to Linear Models
nodes.statement: $\nabla^2 \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{loss}(w^T x_i, y_i) = \frac{1}{n} X^T \mathrm{diag}(\beta) X$, with $\beta_i := \left.\frac{\partial^2 \mathrm{loss}(z,y_i)}{\partial z^2}\right|_{z=y_i}$.
nodes.statement_clean: Hessian of linear ERM is a fixed quadratic form, independent of $w$.

nodes.name: Explaining generalization of overparameterized neural networks
nodes.statement: Identify a complexity measure or property that distinguishes neural networks with small generalization error from architecturally similar networks that generalize poorly, despite having far more parameters than samples.
nodes.statement_clean: Find a principled explanation of why deep nets generalize.

nodes.name: Finite-sample representation by depth-2 ReLU network
nodes.statement: Determine the smallest depth-2 ReLU network (in number of weights) that can represent every function $f: S \to \mathbb{R}$ on every $n$-point sample $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$.
nodes.statement_clean: How many weights does a 2-layer ReLU need to fit any labeling of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$?

nodes.name: Finite-sample expressivity of two-layer ReLU networks (Theorem 1)
nodes.statement: There exists a two-layer neural network with ReLU activations and $2n + d$ weights that can represent any function on a sample of size $n$ in $d$ dimensions.
nodes.statement_clean: A two-layer ReLU net with $2n+d$ weights can fit any labeling of any $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$.
conclusions: There exist $a \in \mathbb{R}^d$, $b, w \in \mathbb{R}^n$ giving a depth-2 ReLU network $c$ with $2n+d$ weights such that $c(z_i) = y_i$ for all $i$

nodes.name: Full rank of interleaving ReLU matrix (Lemma 1)
nodes.statement: For any two interleaving sequences $b_1 < x_1 < b_2 < x_2 < \cdots < b_n < x_n$, the $n \times n$ matrix $A = [\max\{x_i - b_j, 0\}]_{ij}$ has full rank, and its smallest eigenvalue is $\min_i (x_i - b_i)$.
nodes.statement_clean: The interleaving ReLU matrix is lower-triangular with positive diagonal, hence invertible.
assumptions: Real numbers satisfying $b_1 < x_1 < b_2 < x_2 < \cdots < b_n < x_n$

nodes.name: Depth-$k$ expressivity with width $O(n/k)$ (Corollary 1)
nodes.statement: For every $k \ge 2$, there exists a neural network with ReLU activations of depth $k$, width $O(n/k)$ and $O(n + d)$ weights that can represent any function on a sample of size $n$ in $d$ dimensions.
nodes.statement_clean: Width-depth tradeoff: depth $k$, width $O(n/k)$, weights $O(n+d)$ suffice for finite-sample expressivity.
conclusions: There exists a depth-$k$ ReLU network with width $O(n/k)$ and $O(n+d)$ weights representing any function on the sample

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: Choose $a, b$ so that $x_i = \langle a, z_i \rangle$ satisfies the interleaving property; apply Lemma 1 to invert $A = [\max\{x_i - b_j, 0\}]_{ij}$; solve $y = Aw$ for the second-layer weights.
nodes.statement_clean: Construct interleaving via $a$ and $b$, then invert the resulting ReLU matrix to fit any $y$.

nodes.name: Define depth-2 ReLU function $c$
nodes.statement: For $w, b \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $a \in \mathbb{R}^d$, define $c(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{n} w_j \max\{\langle a, x \rangle - b_j, 0\}$, expressible as a depth-2 ReLU network.

nodes.name: Choose $a, b$ to enforce interleaving
nodes.statement: Pick $a \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and $b \in \mathbb{R}^n$ so that $x_i = \langle a, z_i \rangle$ satisfy $b_1 < x_1 < b_2 < \cdots < b_n < x_n$; possible because the $z_i$ are distinct.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 1 to obtain invertible $A$
nodes.statement: By Lemma 1, the matrix $A = [\max\{x_i - b_j, 0\}]_{ij}$ has full rank under the interleaving property.

nodes.name: Solve $y = Aw$ for second-layer weights
nodes.statement: Since $c(z_i) = (Aw)_i$, the linear system $y = Aw$ has a unique solution $w$ that realizes $c(z_i) = y_i$ for all $i$, completing the construction with $2n+d$ weights.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: $A$ is lower triangular with strictly positive diagonal entries $\max\{x_i - b_i, 0\} > 0$, hence invertible; eigenvalues equal the diagonal entries, so $\lambda_{\min}(A) = \min_i (x_i - b_i)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Lower-triangular with positive diagonal $\Rightarrow$ full rank with eigenvalues on diagonal.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Corollary 1 (width-depth tradeoff)
nodes.statement: Partition $[0,1]$ into $b$ intervals each holding $n/b$ projected points; apply the Theorem 1 construction at each layer and combine outputs through ReLU-based interval indicators, yielding depth $b+c$ and width $O(n/b)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Layerwise partition + indicator multiplexer trades width for depth.

nodes.name: Partition $[0,1]$ into $b$ intervals
nodes.statement: Assume w.l.o.g. $x_1, \dots, x_n \in [0,1]$ and partition into disjoint intervals $I_1, \dots, I_b$, each containing $n/b$ points.

nodes.name: Apply Theorem 1 construction per layer
nodes.statement: At layer $j$, apply the depth-2 construction of Theorem 1 to the $n/b$ points in $I_j$, requiring $O(n/b)$ nodes.

nodes.name: Combine layer outputs via ReLU indicators
nodes.statement: Implement (approximate) indicator functions $f_j$ for each interval $I_j$ via constant-size ReLU subnetworks and output $\sum_{j=1}^{b} f_j(x) o_j$, yielding depth $b+c$ and width $O(n/b)$ for total size $O(n+d)$.

nodes.name: Fitting random labels on CIFAR10
nodes.statement: Inception, AlexNet and MLPs trained on CIFAR10 with completely random labels reach $\sim 100\%$ training accuracy and $\sim 10\%$ test accuracy (random guessing), with the same hyperparameters as on true labels.
nodes.statement_clean: Standard CIFAR10 architectures memorize random labels with no hyperparameter changes.

nodes.name: Fitting random pixels and Gaussian noise on CIFAR10
nodes.statement: Replacing CIFAR10 inputs by shuffled pixels, per-image random pixel permutations, or Gaussian noise (matched mean/variance) still yields zero training error for the tested networks.
nodes.statement_clean: CNNs fit even noise-only inputs to zero training error.

nodes.name: Random labels on ImageNet (Inception V3)
nodes.statement: Inception V3 trained on ImageNet with random labels reaches $95.20\%$ top-1 training accuracy on a million random labels from $1000$ classes without hyperparameter tuning; $\sim 90\%$ even with explicit regularizers on.
nodes.statement_clean: Inception V3 nearly memorizes 1M random ImageNet labels.

nodes.name: Partially corrupted labels on CIFAR10
nodes.statement: Varying the label-corruption probability $p$ from $0$ to $1$ on CIFAR10 leaves training error at zero throughout, while test error grows continuously toward random-guessing as $p \to 1$.
nodes.statement_clean: Training error stays $0$; generalization error grows smoothly with corruption $p$.

nodes.name: Effect of data augmentation, weight decay, dropout (Table 1)
nodes.statement: Toggling data augmentation and weight decay on CIFAR10 changes test accuracy of Inception/AlexNet/MLPs by only a few percent; all models still generalize well with all explicit regularizers turned off.
nodes.statement_clean: Explicit regularizers help by a small margin; removing them still leaves good generalization.

nodes.name: Early stopping and batch normalization on Inception
nodes.statement: On ImageNet, early stopping can recover several points of generalization when other regularizers are off; on CIFAR10, batch normalization stabilizes training and improves generalization by $3\sim 4\%$ but is not the source of generalization.
nodes.statement_clean: Implicit regularizers (early stopping, batchnorm) give modest, not fundamental, gains.

nodes.name: Kernel methods on MNIST and CIFAR10 (Table 3)
nodes.section: 5 Implicit Regularization: An Appeal to Linear Models
nodes.statement: Solving $XX^T \alpha = y$ with no regularization gives $1.2\%$ test error on raw MNIST, $0.6\%$ with Gabor preprocessing, $46\%$ on raw CIFAR10, and $17\%$ with random conv-net features; adding $\ell_2$ regularization barely changes the outcome.
nodes.statement_clean: Unregularized kernel solutions generalize well on MNIST/CIFAR10.

nodes.name: Norms of minimum-norm MNIST kernel solutions
nodes.section: 5 Implicit Regularization: An Appeal to Linear Models
nodes.statement: On MNIST, the $\ell_2$-norm of the minimum-norm kernel solution is $\approx 220$ for raw pixels and $\approx 390$ after Gabor preprocessing, yet the latter halves the test error, so minimum-norm magnitude is not predictive of generalization.
nodes.statement_clean: Bigger-norm Gabor solution generalizes better than smaller-norm raw solution.

nodes.name: Rademacher and VC bounds become vacuous under randomization
nodes.statement: Since the tested networks fit random $\pm 1$ labels perfectly, $\hat{R}_n(H) \approx 1$, giving only a trivial bound; the same reasoning makes VC-dimension and fat-shattering dimension uninformative for these classes.
nodes.statement_clean: Empirical Rademacher complexity saturates at 1 for these networks; classical bounds are vacuous.

nodes.name: Uniform stability cannot distinguish true vs random labels
nodes.statement: Uniform stability is a property of the algorithm only and does not depend on the label distribution, so it cannot separate networks with low generalization error (true labels) from those with high error (random labels).
nodes.statement_clean: Algorithm-only stability ignores labels and so cannot explain the gap.

nodes.name: SGD-from-zero converges to minimum $\ell_2$-norm interpolant
nodes.section: 5 Implicit Regularization: An Appeal to Linear Models
nodes.statement: For linear models with $w_0 = 0$, SGD updates $w_{t+1} = w_t - \eta_t e_t x_{i_t}$ keep $w \in \mathrm{span}(\{x_i\})$, so the interpolating solution from SGD coincides with the minimum-$\ell_2$-norm solution of $Xw = y$.
nodes.statement_clean: SGD from zero implicitly selects the minimum-norm interpolant.

nodes.name: Width-depth tradeoff not realized by the depth-2 construction
nodes.statement: The depth-2 construction in Theorem 1 has width $n$; the appendix shows it can be traded for depth, achieving width $O(n/k)$ with depth $k$ (Corollary 1).
nodes.statement_clean: Depth-2 has large width; depth $k$ allows width $O(n/k)$.

nodes.name: Hardt-Recht-Singer SGD stability bound (cited)
nodes.statement: An upper bound on the generalization error of a model trained with SGD in terms of the number of gradient steps, derived via uniform stability.
nodes.statement_clean: Cited bound: gen. error of SGD scales with number of steps via uniform stability.

nodes.name: Bartlett fat-shattering bound (cited)
nodes.statement: For multilayer perceptrons with sigmoid activations, the fat-shattering dimension is bounded in terms of the $\ell_1$-norm of the weights at each node, yielding size-independent generalization bounds.
nodes.statement_clean: Cited: fat-shattering dim of sigmoid MLPs bounded by $\ell_1$ weight norms.

nodes.name: Livni-Shalev-Shamir finite-sample expressivity (cited)
nodes.statement: There exist neural networks with $O(dn)$ parameters that can represent any function on a sample of size $n$ in $d$ dimensions.
nodes.statement_clean: Cited: prior $O(dn)$-parameter finite-sample expressivity result.
